Physics: Coverage is broad and well spread across mechanics, electromagnetism, optics and modern physics, and every key I could verify independently (q2–q8, q11–q13, q16–q19, q22–q28, q30, q32, q33, q35, q37–q40) is correct with clean, well-separated distractors. The level, however, leans easy: q10, q21, q31 and q39 are one-line recall or substitution items, while only q2, q3 and q9 require real multi-step work, so the section under-tests sustained 90-second problem solving. Tighten the two redundant pairs (q8/q17 and q15/q31) and upgrade two of the trivial items to keep the paper's difficulty profile consistent.

[minor] The phrase "its clockwise induced emf is $+0.030$ V" awkwardly mixes a circulation sense with a sign; reword as "the induced emf has magnitude 0.030 V and drives current clockwise" (the sign is irrelevant to what is asked).

[minor] This is the same constant-volume "wire drawn to n times its length" trick as q8, with the same n² answer structure, so one of the pair should be swapped for a different current-electricity item (e.g. a network or meter-bridge problem).

[minor] A single-step $v=u-gt$ substitution that is below BITSAT level and overlaps the vertical-projection kinematics already tested properly in q27; make it demand something more (e.g. a time after the ball has reversed, so speed vs velocity matters).

[minor] Like q15 it only asks the candidate to name a gate from its input–output table (here the textbook NOR pattern), duplicating that skill with no circuit reasoning; replace it or convert it into a gate-circuit analysis with a different target.

Chemistry: The section is broadly balanced across physical, inorganic and organic chemistry and most numerical items (photon energy, ΔU–ΔH, Kp/Kc, Kohlrausch, density, Fischer configurations) are clean, single-step and well within the 90-second budget. Level is uneven at the edges: a few pure recall items (ampicillin class, vitamin–deficiency) are trivial while the lanthanoid ground-multiplet question is far too advanced, and there is needless repetition of VSEPR shape assignment and of ΔTf/van't Hoff-factor problems. Fixing the wording slips in the Lucas, Cannizzaro and nitration items and replacing the two overlaps would make the section print-ready.

[minor] The dangling "respectively" plus the added instruction "Give each pair in low-to-high pH order" is redundant and clumsy; rewrite as "What are the net charges on aspartic acid and lysine at a pH well below all their pKa values and at a pH well above them (in that order)?"

[minor] The stem already states that B³⁺ occupies half the octahedral voids, so asking "what fraction of octahedral voids is occupied" is self-answering; ask instead for the fraction of tetrahedral voids filled (1/8).
[minor] "At room temperature" contradicts the keyed response "only on heating" for the 1° alcohol; either drop the temperature clause or word the 1° entry as "no turbidity at room temperature".
[minor] Distractor (B) names a non-existent species, "bis(4-methoxybenzyl) 4-methoxybenzoate"; the Tishchenko product should be written as 4-methoxybenzyl 4-methoxybenzoate.

[minor] The phrase "major product of monosubstitution" clashes with four dinitro options and leaves the substrate unclear — name it in the stem (e.g. 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene), since if the figure were bromobenzene the o/p-directing Br would make key D wrong.
[minor] This duplicates Q71's skill (extracting a van't Hoff factor from ΔTf of a cobalt–ammine complex); replace one of the pair with a different colligative or equilibrium application.
[minor] This tests essentially the same VSEPR shape/lone-pair assignment as Q48 (and even reuses a xenon fluoride); swap it for a different bonding concept such as bond order/MO or dipole moment.

[major] Obtaining μ = 0 for Eu³⁺ requires the ⁷F₀ ground term and spin–orbit (L–S) coupling, which is well beyond the BITSAT/NCERT level where only spin-only moments are used, so the keyed answer is not reachable in 90 s.

English Proficiency: The section covers the expected spread — synonyms, antonyms, idiom, preposition/grammar error spotting, sentence improvement, rearrangement, vocabulary completion and a two-question RC set — and all keys are defensible with no data or figure inconsistencies. Difficulty is uneven, though: q88 and q92 are the only items with real discriminative power, while q86 and q89 are giveaways and several grammar items are routine. Replacing the trivial jumble and lifting the easiest completion would give the section a more appropriate BITSAT level within the 90-second-per-item budget.

[major] The three sentences are explicitly signposted "First / Next / A few weeks later", so the order is given away without any reasoning, making the item far too trivial and a duplicate of the genuine rearrangement skill already tested in q92.

[minor] "Greeted them with a warm smile" plus three uniformly negative distractors makes the key obvious at a primary-school level; the sentence needs a subtler contrast cue to be worth a BITSAT slot.
[minor] The item is a word-analogy (antonym pair), not "Sentence Completion (vocabulary)" as tagged, so the section label should be corrected to Analogies.

Logical Reasoning: Only eight of the ten items are actually usable, since both figure-based questions (97, 102) ship without artwork and the syllogism (99) hinges on a restated premise. The surviving items are almost all single-step alphabet or word tasks (dictionary order, +3 shift, letter positions, bird/fish classification, one-line blood relation), so the section sits well below BITSAT difficulty and offers little discrimination. Rebalance by restoring the two figure items and replacing one or two of the trivial ones with a multi-step seating/arrangement or data-sufficiency question.
[major] The four option figures are entirely absent, so the odd-figure-out item has no content and the key B cannot be verified.

[major] Conclusion I is a word-for-word restatement of the second premise, which under the common convention that a mere restatement is not a valid conclusion makes option D equally defensible; replace it with a genuine inference such as "Some readers are poets."
[major] The figure carrying the numbers is missing, leaving no data from which the missing value (key 15) could be deduced.

Mathematics: Every key in the section checks out on recomputation, and coverage of algebra, coordinate geometry, 3D, vectors and calculus is broadly sensible, though integral calculus (five items) and sets/relations/functions (four) are over-weighted against trigonometry. The difficulty profile is bottom-heavy: roughly a dozen items (106, 110, 118, 119, 120, 122, 126, 128, 149, 150) are one-step plug-ins, with only 121, 133, 137 and 140 requiring genuine multi-step work inside 90 s. Fix the figure-dependent item 138 and promote two or three of the trivial recall items to standard BITSAT two-step level.

[major] The keyed answer depends entirely on an arrow diagram whose ordered pairs are nowhere specified in the item, so option A cannot be verified (and "S is reflexive only" is loose phrasing for "reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive").
[minor] Solving sin 2x = 0 is a single-step textbook recall well below BITSAT discrimination level; replace with e.g. sin 2x = cos x or add a restricted-interval root count.
[minor] The profit data are given as bare numbers ("5 per stool") while the stem asks for dollars, so state the currency once with the data and use rupees for consistency with an Indian paper.
